# Relative Helly bound controlled by the largest fiber dimension

The following results use ordinary finite-dimensional Helly and Doignon's theorem, but do not assume Oertel's conjecture.

Let n,d>=0. Put Lambda=Z^n x R^d. Let C be a compact convex subset of R^{n+d}, not necessarily a full-dimensional body, and suppose S=C intersect Lambda is nonempty. Assume every nonempty integer fiber C_z has affine dimension at most q, where 0<=q<=d.

For n=0, interpret Z^0 as the singleton zero-dimensional space and 2^n=1.

## Lemma 1: finite relative Helly bound

For every finite family K_1,...,K_m of closed convex subsets of R^{n+d}, if

S intersect K_1 intersect ... intersect K_m is empty,

then some subfamily of at most h=2^n(q+1) of the K_i already has empty intersection with S.

Proof. For every index subset I subset {1,...,m} with |I|<=q+1, including I=empty, set

P_I=pi(C intersect intersection_{i in I} K_i),

where pi is projection onto the first n coordinates. Each P_I is compact and convex, possibly empty: the set being projected is closed in compact C and convex. In particular P_empty=pi(C).

We claim that an integer z belongs to every P_I if and only if the full fiber intersection C_z intersect intersection_{i=1}^m (K_i)_z is nonempty.

The reverse direction is immediate. For the forward direction, membership in P_empty ensures C_z is nonempty. Write r=dim aff(C_z)<=q. The convex sets C_z intersect (K_i)_z are subsets of the r-dimensional affine space aff(C_z). For every subfamily of at most r+1 of these sets, the index set I has |I|<=q+1, and membership of z in P_I says their intersection is nonempty. Ordinary Helly in that affine space gives a nonempty full intersection. The assertion also holds when r=0 or m<r+1: the small-subfamily conditions then include the full family.

By the hypothesized infeasibility, the finite family of convex sets P_I has intersection disjoint from Z^n. Doignon's theorem yields at most 2^n index subsets I_1,...,I_k such that

Z^n intersect P_{I_1} intersect ... intersect P_{I_k} is empty.

Put J=I_1 union ... union I_k. Then |J|<=2^n(q+1). If some point of S belonged to all K_j for j in J, its integer projection would belong to every selected P_{I_l}, a contradiction. This proves the lemma.

For n=0 the Doignon step needs no external theorem: each P_I is either empty or the single point of R^0, and an empty total intersection forces one P_I to be empty.

## Lemma 2: arbitrary-measure centerpoint on S

Let mu be any finite positive Borel measure on R^{n+d} supported on S, and normalize mu(S)=1. Then there exists a single point y in S such that every closed ambient halfspace H containing y satisfies

mu(H)>=1/[2^n(q+1)].

Proof. Apply the compact closed-halfspace intersection argument from accepted fact 6d6fcf377e68c79c with h=2^n(q+1). Lemma 1 above supplies exactly the finite closed-convex intersection bound needed in that argument; compactness of S supplies the infinite-family step. The same inner approximation of the open complement by closed halfspaces retains all boundary mass. The arbitrary-measure centerpoint mechanism is existing background; the new input is the maximal-fiber-dimension bound in Lemma 1.

## Corollary 3: intrinsic centerpoint bound

Let C be as above and q=dim_H(S). Since S is a finite union of compact convex fibers, q is the maximum affine dimension of its fibers, and 0<H_q(S)<infinity. Applying Lemma 2 to mu=H_q restricted to S / H_q(S) gives

max_{y in S} depth_S(y)>=1/[2^n(q+1)].

The same bound holds for every finite positive weighted measure supported on S, regardless of the relative weights of the fibers.

## Corollary 4: OC for all q<=1

For q=0, the bound is 2^{-n}, which is at least 2^{-n}gamma_d for every d>=0.

For q=1, necessarily d>=1. The bound is 2^{-(n+1)}. The binomial theorem gives (1+1/d)^d>=1+d(1/d)=2, so gamma_d=(d/(d+1))^d<=1/2. This proves the required bound 2^{-n}gamma_d.

In particular, OC holds unconditionally for every n when d=0 or d=1, and for every n,d when the intrinsic dimension of the intersection is at most one. When n=0 the convex-body hypothesis forces q=d; q=0 with positive ambient dimension is then impossible, while q=1 is the ordinary interval case.

## Scope of the proved statement

The assumptions needed for Lemma 1 are compact convex C, finite closed convex test families, and the uniform bound q on all nonempty integer-fiber dimensions. The compactness of the P_I is why the proof was stated for closed K_i. Lemma 2 uses only closed test halfspaces and handles open complements through explicit inner approximation. There is no unproved extension to arbitrary open convex test sets.

For q>=2, the general constant 1/(q+1) is below gamma_d when d=q, so this alone does not prove OC. It does prove OC whenever gamma_d<=1/(q+1), for the specified q,d. Any dimension induction seeking the full bound must supply an additional geometric argument beyond this relative Helly estimate.
